statementIssues.note: Says the authors described using sensors to track asymmetries "that guide phase progression"; the source says they "can be used to guide" progression, a proposal rather than a tested practice.
"None ... follows outcomes after a combined criterion is applied" slightly understates 705, which did follow RTC and reinjury after a criteria-based process, though without comparison.
The asymmetry digest (C11) addresses asymmetry in general sport populations; applying it to post-injury limb-symmetry interpretation is a transfer the brief does not flag.

tierNote: Limited is appropriate: no source tests a combination rule, evidence is a systematic review, uncontrolled ACL case series and single case. No recommendation was given (recommendedDirection null) and actions are framed as descriptive options.
usefulnessNote: Honest and accurate about the gap, with clear guardrails keeping clearance with clinicians. It underuses the most decision-relevant evidence in its own sources: 705 reports final-stage on-field GPS outputs versus team-training demands (TD 106%, HID 104%, PS 88%, ACC 110%, DEC 48%), which directly informs readiness for modified team practice, and 396 notes cutting and deceleration are hard to reach in individual phases. Movement quality is barely addressed.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When a source reports outputs relative to the target activity (for example field loads versus team-training demands), surface them for questions about advancing to that activity.
Cover each signal named in the practical question (here movement quality) or state explicitly that the pack has nothing on it.
Preserve modal verbs from source text ('can be used to guide') rather than converting proposals into described practice.
Flag when evidence about a general population (healthy-athlete asymmetry) is applied to an injured or rehabilitation population.
